1:
On my first day back in Beijing, I opened the piece I made on my first day in Berlin.

As I wrote another track, it felt as though time was somehow responding to itself.

Winter - spring.
A long, long wait for myself.

This, too, was the first ritual of unfolding.
2:
The first ritual, an underground world.
A journey of descent.

Slowly, a little emerges.
3:
The journey into the underworld always begins in the basement of a house.

Down there are memories we haven’t paid attention to in a very long time. But they’ve always been there, in our home. We’ve just almost forgotten about them.

This is how we accidentally forget so many things. But our bodies remember everything.

None of this can be measured in linear time.

Will we catch a glimpse of light?
4:
When I was little, I used to play a game called MapleStory. Sometimes it feels childish to talk about it now, but these things are all part of our memories.

There was a place in the game called Kerning City. The people there somehow felt just like the kind of adventure I imagined as a child.

I just remembered that I used to dream about this game, even when I was in university.

And it’s only now that I remember.
5: Memory wanders in circles, always climbing and descending. A spiral staircase. If possible, when it is heard, how many people will step into such a ritual and hear their own memories? Perhaps this is an invitation, a journey.
6:
One from within another.
One taken away.
One placed inside another.

Which one is it?
And which one are we?
7:
Today I want to respond to it.
Is something at the bottom overlapping again — what is a similar experience?
It passes through me and relates to another.
My will lies between them.

(Listening after the mix was done)
I heard a ship sailing on through the sound of a horn; if where we are heading is an iceberg, it seems we would simply drift slowly toward it.
8:
When something that was once hidden becomes the main focus, the story it unfolds is completely different.

In this piece, I brought a sound that had been sitting at the very bottom of an earlier fragment all the way to the front. Even the images that seem to exist on the margins have something of their own to say.

(After finishing the mix)

I heard the desire underneath.
9:
In the process of this dialogue, there were long stretches of waiting and moments of playing alone. And that long, open space began to reveal itself too.

(After finishing the mix)

I realized that I’m no longer the same person I was back then, and everything I hear now is completely different. I almost forgot that I was the one who made this. Or maybe I never really was.
10:
The first piece in which my voice appears, but not as the main one — as the solo of a looping instrument. I am only one small link in it, playing together with them against that tangled background.

5.12
Before sending it to the group, I'll listen to this music once more. New feelings may surface too. It's like inviting different people to witness a ritual, starting with those who find their own family.
11:
The first and the eleventh started interacting with each other. I never would have imagined that these two could come together so harmoniously.

It wasn’t something I could have planned or imagined beforehand. It was only when I put them together that I discovered this, and it really surprised me.

(At this point, I suddenly felt like extending an invitation to the group.

If you have time, maybe you could try listening to one piece a day, rather than listening to them all at once. Let the echoes of one piece stay with you for a while before moving on to the next.

There’s something about patience in this, and about giving ourselves space to feel what we’ve heard.

Maybe we could do something similar when we finally release the project. Lighting up one fragment each day, documenting what that moment of illumination looks like, until all 108 fragments have appeared.

(I need to tell Hui about this.)
12:
Suddenly, rhythms and musical textures appeared that I would never have explored before. Is this what it feels like to move from one stage into another?

When a sound I’ve never encountered before enters my life, at first I can’t find a place for it.

It’s also about whether I can allow this temporary “disharmony” to keep growing, and let it be heard as part of the response, too.
13:
From this point on, I could clearly feel that as I was responding to them, I was no longer their author. They had begun to affect me. They had lives of their own.

There was something mourning in this piece, while new memories were also arriving.

(In the days after finishing the mix, I began to realize that perhaps the art we are making is a way of blessing, mourning, or loving something that is absent, invisible, or not allowed to exist.

With the sounds and love that emerge from the cracks, we respond to the rumbling deep beneath our memories.

Those memories that want us to forget them, yet also want to be remembered.

Forgetting and remembering again are speaking to each other. 5.12）
14:
How do we allow the responses between us to be intermittent, to move through a process of tuning in and out? How do we make room for the things that don’t quite connect, and acknowledge them as part of memory too?

I realized that the bass in this piece sounds a little like the bass in the Egg, a song I released some time ago. That was something I hadn’t expected either.

Throughout this process, I had assumed that each response would have to carry something from the previous piece. But I began to realize that this was just a rule I had made up for what could be understood as a response.

When I actually started working with them, I found that they were participating in and responding to one another in ways I could never have imagined.

(April)
15:
Response. I’m starting to feel that I don’t really like this word anymore. I still prefer correspondence.

The correspondence has moved into a much larger space, like an underground world of water. Without someone carrying a light, perhaps it would go unheard.

A ritual of bringing a little light into the darkness.

(After finishing the mix, I happened to be thinking about communication between people, or perhaps between people and the world.

I began to realize that communication is something that runs through everything. The way our bodies communicate, the way music communicates, and the ways they themselves interact with the world.

Perhaps these interactions also affect us, and we are learning from each of them, one by one.)
16:
I saw the deep blue sky at dusk, the kind of blue where you can’t tell whether it’s dawn or dusk.

I tried to take a photo of it, but I couldn’t capture that color to share with anyone. You had to be there, standing in that very place, with your body, just looking.

On the stairs on my way home, my body began to respond to something I had written before. Was it 13, or 14, or 12? I couldn’t even remember which one it was anymore.

As I kept climbing, my breathing became more and more uneven. By the end, I couldn’t even tell which sound it was.

But something had happened between us, somewhere along that long, steep climb home.
17:
What does the distance between us and war feel like?

Compared to before, that distance seems to have grown smaller.

How is this awareness shaping the way we live?
18:
The call from within the collective has always been there, somewhere in our memories.

The East. A fire is lit. A sacred tower rising from the water.

Eagles, flying tigers, pythons, bears, wild boars, hedgehogs, giant whales, leopards.

Symbols of good fortune and blessings hanging from the sacred tree, one by one, in abundance, until the whole tree is full.
19:
A simple letter back.
I watched a film today and felt like sending a little piece of it back to yesterday. Just that simple.
Throughout this process, I kept doubting myself. I know there are so many other voices influencing me, asking, can it really be this simple?
Why is it becoming harder and harder for us to trust the simplest things?
Sometimes it’s just a few breaths and heartbeats.
When I got to this point, I felt the urge to keep adding more and more things that weren’t really needed, almost as if I were trying to explain my own music.
I noticed this, and let it unfold as it was.
20:
Can different versions of “me” play together?
Coming from different memories.
When they come together, they remain different. Even the parts that don’t quite harmonize can still resonate with one another.
21: There are afternoons like that, when everything in the air rises and bubbles upward in stillness; in summer the air above is warm, a longing to rise slowly, rather than a desire to shoot straight up.
23:
The present time and September 2, 2022
Memories are all twisted together. A wet towel.
24:
What I feel in my body today is mourning.

I don’t know why these things are here, but they’re all showing up in the music, one by one.

Just listening, quietly.
25: When the first people arrived here, they knew nothing, and didn't know that they didn't know. What they had was endless curiosity, mouths hanging open. Where are we going?
26:
At first, we couldn’t see each other. When we began to recognize one another, “I” and “you” became separate. The moment we met was also the first moment of separation.

That was the piece about an expedition.

Today, I went to a screening of a film made by Juliette Binoche, followed by a conversation with her. She talked about how her film was an adventure, and how she invited the audience to become creators themselves, to find their own ways of understanding, feeling, and thinking, rather than being told what to think or having everything explained to them.

I could really relate to that feeling.

Creating excites me, but it also brings up some of my deepest fears. I often question whether the frequency I’m on might be misunderstood by others.

But this is something I have to move through.

To keep sharing this process, carrying both the uneasiness and the love. To allow myself to be vulnerable, and perhaps, through that, give others a chance to recognize that they can allow their own vulnerability too.

And somewhere in all of this, in all of this, to keep going deeper.

Further down, and down.

Always.
27: Tomorrow I'll have a tooth pulled. I've written a sacrificial song for the little tooth and drawn some portraits of it for its funeral. A simple blessing and farewell. Feeling loss. Early people gathered around to bless and perform rituals. Our lives need everyday awareness. reconnect remember
28:
After having a tooth pulled, a frequency that makes my teeth ache.

Some feelings of absurdity and vulnerability. A little playfulness, a little mockery.

The seriousness of losing something. And the way I used to respond to pain as a child, screaming, or making little gagging sounds.

I remembered all of it, and it was all happening at the same time.

Brief, powerful memories. Deep, yet somehow light.

I began to realize that everything is asking us how we want to live, and where we want to go.

We practice being with the things we’ve never allowed to exist.

This takes courage, and a willingness to venture into the unknown.
29:
The maxillary sinus is a space, an enclosed space within the bones.

There are melodies in there too, carrying the wish to heal.

Waiting to get better, with the same sincerity and childlike hope as waiting for Santa Claus to leave a present in a Christmas stocking.
30: When I perform, I always turn off the metronome, and I don't intend to align those small rhythmic misalignments. Perhaps you on the other side can hear that someone is playing for you — a person, with their own fear, panic or hesitation.
31:
Letters That Cannot Align

Ryuichi Sakamoto kept composing right up until the end of his life. In the last pieces he created, you can really hear the sighs of an entire life, one after another. A sigh can’t simply be defined by any words. A sigh is eternal. There’s something deeply moving about that feeling of being alive.

Staying connected to that source, bringing out those unstable feelings from somewhere deep underneath, one by one, day by day. Perhaps someone really will hear that vastness.

In his final concert, the notes he played weren’t perfect… They were trembling, one after another. But each note was an incredibly precise expression of where he was in that very moment.

I suddenly realized that if I could speak these things from somewhere deep inside me, perhaps there would be a chance to invite more people to join through that website.

I’ve stopped for a while because of my cat’s tumor and my own surgery. Life always seems to be hanging by a thread.

When I sing, if I can hear the ensemble happening in the space around me, my breath becomes longer and longer. But if I focus only on my own breathing, it becomes shorter and shallower. Even when I want it to be longer.

Perhaps the only thing we can really do is make more space, and listen to the ensemble.

66 asked me what I would do if I found myself unable to communicate within a group.

I said it’s something I know intuitively. Art gives us space. Whenever there’s something I want to say but can’t put into words, I can turn it into a ritual or an action.

But in a way, it’s the same. There still has to be that moment of opening up, of beginning to speak.

I said that moment is an unstructured moment. There’s a subtle sense of danger, and space to experience failure. And that space for failure is incredibly important.

At this point in my life, I’m made up almost entirely of all kinds of ongoing failures.

I’m willing to fail completely, in every single moment.

I wasn’t willing to do that before.
32:
Shaozi is sick.

Shaozi is a language of love. She is my only family.

So many different things are tangled together here. And when none of them can really be put into words, it is no longer about describing something.

It becomes a way of being.
33:
After landing in Haikou, I wrote this while sitting at the airport, waiting for someone I’m traveling with to arrive from another city.

The sounds of the airport hall, and the warm, humid feeling of this city already settling on my skin.

The same announcements repeating, new information coming through the speakers.

What kinds of memories might all of this bring to the surface?

When people come together, there’s a sense of all the possibilities that can begin to flow. As if the horns of fate are sounding.

A space where each of us plays along with it, our sounds meeting and coming together.
